introduction-power-user-tools.core: Beyond add, commit and push, Git has power tools for the hard 10% of situations: worktrees for parallel work, bisect run for automated bug hunts, rerere for repeated conflicts, and submodules or subtrees for embedding repositories.

first_principles.problem: The hard cases (an urgent hotfix mid-feature, mystery regressions, recurring conflicts, shared code) are where teams lose the most time.
truths: Most daily work uses a few commands.
Rare situations cost the most time.
Git already has tools for them.

analogy.title: A Swiss army knife's hidden blades
analogy.story: Most people only use the main blade; the hidden tools save the day in unusual situations.
analogy.breaks: Power tools add complexity, so use them when the situation calls for it.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Each problem gets a precise tool.

check.q: Which tool lets you work on two branches simultaneously?

git-worktree-parallel-universes.core: `git worktree add` creates extra working directories attached to the same repository, each on its own branch, so you can hotfix main without stashing or disturbing your feature work.

first_principles.problem: An urgent bug arrives mid-feature, and you have to stash, switch, rebuild and later restore, losing context and build caches.
truths: One working directory holds one checkout.
The object database can be shared.
Context switches are costly.
derivation: Each directory gets its **own branch and files**.
They **share objects and refs**, so it's cheap.
The same branch can't be checked out twice.

analogy.title: Multiple dressing rooms
analogy.story: Instead of changing outfits in one room, you walk into a second room already set up with the other outfit.
analogy.breaks: Each worktree still needs its own dependency installs and build directories.

example.title: Hotfix without stashing

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The feature build and editor state stay intact.

code.text:
git worktree add ../app-hotfix -b hotfix/login main
cd ../app-hotfix && fix && git commit -am fix && git push
cd - # back to feature, untouched

example.outcome: parallel work with no context loss.

check.q: Can two worktrees have the same branch checked out?
check.a: No. Git prevents a branch being checked out in more than one worktree.

managing-worktrees.core: Manage worktrees with Git commands: `list`, `remove` and `prune`. Deleting the directory by hand leaves stale metadata in .git/worktrees.

first_principles.problem: After `rm -rf`, Git still thinks the worktree exists, and the branch looks 'checked out elsewhere'.
truths: Worktrees are tracked in .git/worktrees.
Removing files doesn't update that metadata.
Stale entries block branch operations.
derivation: **`git worktree remove <path>`** to delete one cleanly.
**`git worktree prune`** to clear stale entries.

analogy.title: Checking out of a hotel properly
analogy.story: Leaving without checking out means the room still shows as occupied in the system.
analogy.breaks: prune only removes entries whose directories are actually gone.

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: The branch is freed and the metadata is clean.

code.text:
git worktree list
git worktree remove ../app-hotfix
git worktree prune   # if someone already rm -rf'd it

check.q: What happens if you rm -rf a worktree directory?
check.a: Git keeps a stale entry, so the branch still appears checked out until you run prune.

git-bisect-run-automated-bug-hunting.core: `git bisect run <script>` automates the binary search: Git checks out each midpoint, runs your script, and treats exit 0 as good, 1–127 as bad and 125 as skip, until it names the culprit commit.

first_principles.problem: Manually testing each bisect step across 200 commits is tedious and error-prone.
truths: Bisect only needs a good/bad verdict at each step.
Scripts can produce that verdict.
Some commits can't be tested (broken builds).
derivation: Write a **test script** that returns the right exit codes.

analogy.title: A robot running the higher/lower game
analogy.story: You give the robot the rules, and it plays every round while you get coffee.
analogy.breaks: Exit codes above 127 abort the bisect, so be careful with signals in the script.

example.title: A failing test somewhere in 200 commits

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: About 8 automated steps name the first bad commit.

code.text:
git bisect start HEAD v1.4.0
git bisect run sh -c 'make build || exit 125; pytest tests/test_auth.py'
git bisect reset

example.outcome: regressions are found while you do something else.

check.q: What does exit code 125 mean in bisect run?
check.a: This commit can't be tested, so skip it.

git-rerere-reuse-recorded-resolution.core: rerere ('reuse recorded resolution') records how you resolved a conflict and replays that resolution automatically when the same conflict reappears.

first_principles.problem: Rebasing a long-lived branch every day brings back the same three conflicts every morning.
truths: Identical conflicts recur across rebases.
A resolution can be recorded and matched.
Repetitive manual work invites mistakes.
derivation: Resolve the conflict **once**; Git records it.
When it **recurs**, Git applies the recorded fix.

analogy.title: A sticky note on a tricky lock
analogy.story: The first time, you work out the trick. Next time the note tells you instantly.
analogy.breaks: If the right resolution has changed, a replayed old one can be wrong, so always review.

example.title: Daily rebase of a feature branch

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Minutes saved every day, and consistent resolutions.

code.text:
git config --global rerere.enabled true
git rebase main   # day 1: resolve conflicts manually
git rebase main   # day 2: 'Resolved using previous resolution'

example.outcome: repeated conflicts stop being repeated work.

check.a: When you repeatedly rebase or merge a long-lived branch that hits the same conflicts.

git-submodules-a-repository-inside-a-rep.core: A submodule embeds another repository as a pointer to an exact commit, so you pin dependencies precisely. The cost is extra commands and easy-to-forget update steps.

first_principles.problem: Five services need a specific, pinned version of a shared auth library that lives in its own repository.
truths: The parent stores a commit hash, not the code.
Pinning gives reproducibility.
Extra steps get forgotten.
derivation: To bump it: update inside the submodule, then **commit the new pointer**.

analogy.title: A bookmark to a specific edition
analogy.story: Your book references the 3rd edition of another book. Readers have to fetch that exact edition themselves.
analogy.breaks: Teammates who forget the submodule commands get empty or stale directories, which is a common source of confusion.

steps.label: Gotcha
steps.detail: Others must run `git submodule update` after pulling.

code.text:
cd libs/auth && git fetch && git checkout v2.3.0 && cd -
git add libs/auth && git commit -m "Bump auth to v2.3.0"

check.q: What does the parent repo store for a submodule?
check.a: The URL and the exact commit SHA of the embedded repository.

git-subtrees-the-alternative.core: A subtree copies the external project's files (and optionally its history) into your repo. Everything is just there on clone, with no extra commands, but syncing upstream is more manual.

first_principles.problem: Submodules confuse contributors who forget the init and update steps.
truths: Copied code needs no extra clone steps.
Copies can drift from upstream.
Pushing changes back upstream takes deliberate effort.

analogy.title: Photocopying the chapter you need
analogy.story: The chapter is now in your binder, readable by anyone, but it won't update when the original book does unless you re-copy it.
analogy.breaks: History can get noisy, and contributing upstream is less natural than with submodules.

example.title: Vendoring a config library

code.text:
git subtree add --prefix=vendor/cfg https://git.example.com/cfg.git main --squash
git subtree pull --prefix=vendor/cfg https://git.example.com/cfg.git main --squash

example.outcome: simpler for consumers, at the cost of syncing work.

check.q: Main advantage of subtree over submodule?
check.a: Clones include the code directly, with no extra submodule commands.
